sentences.text: The snout of Cerrejonisuchus is the shortest of all dyrosaurids, measuring only 54-59% of the total skull length.
This snout is narrow and maintains a consistent width from the nostrils to the eye sockets, with the nostrils located at the very tip.
The animal possessed generally uniform teeth, though the third upper jaw tooth was enlarged and the fourth was smaller, and unlike many relatives, these teeth were not curved.
Cerrejonisuchus was the smallest known dyrosaur in terms of estimated body length and held the record for the shortest snout of any dyrosaurid.
Fossil evidence suggests this small crocodylomorph may have served as a secondary food source for the giant snake Titanoboa in their shared habitat.
The genus Cerrejonisuchus was described by Hastings et al. in 2010 based on fossils found in the Cerrejón Formation in northeastern Colombia.
Specimens were discovered in the Cerrejón open-pit coal mine at Mina La Puente, including a holotype skull, lower jaws, a skull with a partial skeleton, and a partial snout.
Its compressed, homodont teeth suggest a terrestrial predatory lifestyle, though its flat skull differs from other terrestrial crocodylomorphs.
The authority for the genus Cerrejonisuchus is Hastings et al., 2010, and the type species is C. improcerus.
A 2010 phylogenetic analysis placed Cerrejonisuchus basally in the dyrosaur clade between Phosphatosaurus and Arambourgisuchus, showing that snout shape does not determine phylogeny in dyrosaurs.
Cerrejonisuchus lived during the Middle to Late Paleocene epoch, specifically from the Selandian to the Thanetian stages, between 61.66 and 56 million years ago.
Fossils were found in sediments likely deposited in a brackish water river-to-lagoonal environment, an age confirmed by carbon isotopes, pollen, spores, and dinoflagellate cysts.
The presence of dyrosaurids like Cerrejonisuchus in Paleocene Colombia suggests a radiation of dyrosaurids in South America following the K–T boundary mass extinction.
